claims.text: Equimolar HfNbTaTiZr has a primarily defect-free BCC structure under the proposed sample conditions.
The applicable HfNbTaTiZr samples contain less than approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Combining DFT-derived force constants with a machine-learning correction will accurately predict lattice thermal conductivity separately from electronic thermal conductivity.
The new approach will reduce prediction error by roughly 30% relative to traditional Debye-based or defect-free simulations.
The approximately 30% error reduction will hold from 200 K to 1200 K.
DFT-informed lattice dynamics can calculate phonon dispersions and scattering rates for HfNbTaTiZr.
A machine-learning correction trained on available experimental data can separate and quantify the lattice contribution independently of electronic heat transport.
Local mass fluctuations and short-range chemical ordering modify phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Computing phonon dispersions and lifetimes and calibrating against experiments decouples lattice heat conduction from electronic contributions.
Conventional Debye or defect-free bulk models ignore force-constant variation and local chemical order relevant to thermal transport.

The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will match independently measured lattice contributions with an error at least 30% lower than that of models that conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Below 200 K, HfNbTaTiZr has a nearly equal or dominant lattice contribution relative to its electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
From 300 K to 1200 K, the total thermal conductivity of the relevant material remains between 10 and 17 W/(K m).
Electronic heat conduction rises between 300 K and 1200 K.
Prior analytical and simulation methods assume perfect, defect-free crystals and simplify or conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
The proposed accuracy is limited to low-impurity, near-single-phase BCC samples between 200 K and 1200 K.
Significant defects, additional phases, or unrecognized scattering mechanisms may eliminate the proposed improvement.
The 30% improvement estimate is based on discrepancies between simple Debye theories and experimental data.
Sample quality, measurement precision, unidentified scattering mechanisms, and temperature-dependent phase changes can alter predictive accuracy.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability range begins at 200 K, but the predicted outcome makes a model prediction for temperatures below 200 K.
